summary: Jon Postel's note on the effect of satellite links on the ARPANET. A satellite path adds much more delay without necessarily lowering the data rate. He notes that interactive use with character-at-a-time remote echo is already marginal on the surface network. He asks users to think about how this affects interactive services.

eli5.summary: A message that goes up to space and back takes much longer than one down a wire. This note warns that talking in real time with a faraway computer will feel slow when satellites are used.

questions: why satellite links hurt remote echo
subtitle: A 1972 warning that satellite links would add large delay to the ARPANET and strain interactive use.

tldr.problem: Satellite transmission links were being considered for the ARPANET, and they would greatly increase delay even if they did not slow the transmission rate.
tldr.mechanism: Jon Postel estimates the added delay from the longer path, points to remote echo and small buffers as trouble spots, and asks for renewed discussion of ways around the delay.
tldr.outcome: The RFC argues that systems already marginal for character-at-a-time remote echo would become unusable with an extra half second of delay.

today: The unit metadata lists the status of RFC 346 as Unknown. It is a 1972 discussion note, and the text does not record what followed.

sections.title: How Much Delay a Satellite Adds
sections.content:
A satellite path will not necessarily change the transmission rate, but it will change the delay. The RFC approximates the change by path length. A synchronous-orbit satellite is about 22,000 miles above the earth, so the path is about 44,000 miles, compared with 3,000 miles in the worst surface case. That is about a 15 to 1 increase in path length and delay.

For light, 3,000 miles takes .016 seconds and 44,000 miles takes .236 seconds.
sections.eli5: Going to space and back is a much longer trip than staying on the ground, so everything arrives later, even if it travels just as fast.

sections.title: Echo and Buffer Problems
sections.content:
In the surface ARPANET of the time, delays already make interactive servers with character-at-a-time remote echo only marginally useful. The author believes this delay (unmeasured) is largely due to the host systems. Adding a half second of transmission delay would make these marginal systems unusable.

Buffers are the second concern. If a receiving system buffers only one line of text and refreshes the allocation as each line is output to a human user, there will be at least a half second delay between lines arriving. That need not be a problem until the output device is above about 150 characters/second, but host delays are estimated at 0.1 second to 1.0 second, so the "small buffer" problem can be expected even with slower devices.
sections.eli5: If you must wait for a reply after every single letter you type, a long delay makes typing miserable. And a tiny mailbox that holds one letter at a time makes the sender wait too.

sections.title: Suggested Discussion
sections.content:
The RFC suggests resuming discussion of ways to get around these delays. Topics could include buffer sizes in servers and users, echo plex techniques, and moving part of the input processing to the user system.

If echo functions are moved to the user system, the author advises aiming for a "standard" package, which turns an M times N problem into an M plus N problem. Readers are pointed to RFC 1 (Crocker), RFC 5 (Rulifson) and RFC 51 (Elie) for earlier thinking.
sections.eli5: He asks everyone to think of fixes, and to agree on one shared fix so each computer does not need its own special one.
